h1: The 6 Best Food Processors Under $200 of 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaTitle: Best Food Processors Under $200: Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: six food processors under $200 from Ninja, Hamilton Beach, KitchenAid and Cuisinart, compared on bowl size, motor and use case.
summary: The Ninja Professional Plus BN601 is the best food processor under $200, with a 1000-peak-watt motor, a 9-cup bowl and Auto-iQ presets. The Hamilton Beach 12-cup is the capacity and value pick. The 10-cup stainless model fits regular prep, the KitchenAid suits brand loyalists, and the Cuisinart handles quick chopping.
intro: Buyers choose a food processor by chasing the biggest bowl and the highest wattage, then discover the machine suits neither their cooking nor their cabinets. A huge bowl turns one onion into a cleanup chore, while a small one forces batches every time you prep a week of meals. The honest question is what you chop most, and how often.

We ranked six food processors under the $200 line from their listings, scoring bowl capacity, motor power and the functions each one lists. We dropped a multi-bowl grinder-style unit and a smaller KitchenAid chopper so every pick here is a true processor or a clearly labeled compact. Where a listing gives no wattage, we say so and do not guess.

products.name: Ninja Professional Plus Food Processor, 1000PW, 9-Cup, BN601
products.verdict: The strongest motor and presets under the $200 cap.
products.description:
The Ninja BN601 earns its spot with the motor. A 1000-peak-watt drive matters because dense jobs such as shredding cheese, grinding nuts or kneading dough stall weaker motors, and Auto-iQ presets run set programs so you do not time pulses by eye. The 9-cup bowl is big enough for family prep, and it sits at the top of the $100 to $200 tier.

It wins because it is the only model here that lists both a strong motor and automatic programs. The Hamilton Beach 12-cup holds three more cups, but lists no wattage, so you cannot compare power at all. Peak watts also run higher than continuous watts, so treat the headline number as a ceiling.

Buy it if you have outgrown a budget machine and want real power. It costs roughly double the Hamilton Beach models, so skip it if you only chop an occasional onion.
products.idealFor: Regular cooks who want a stronger motor.
products.skipIf: You only chop an occasional onion.

products.name: Hamilton Beach 12 Cup Stack & Snap Food Processor and Vegetable Chopper
products.verdict: The biggest bowl here at a mid-range price.
products.description:
Hamilton Beach's 12-cup Stack & Snap is the capacity champion. The bowl is the largest in the ranking, a vegetable chopper mode handles quick jobs, and Stack & Snap assembly means no twist locks to line up. Tool-free assembly sounds minor until you put the machine together twice a week.

It ranks second because it delivers more volume than the Ninja for far less money, in the $50 to $100 tier. The tradeoff is information: no wattage and no presets are listed, so power on dense ingredients is an open question. Against the 10-cup model below, you gain two cups at a similar price.

Choose it for batch cooking, big salads and weekly meal prep. The caveat is storage: a 12-cup bowl and its lid take real cabinet space. Skip it if your kitchen is tight or your cooking is mostly small portions.

products.name: Hamilton Beach Food Processor & Vegetable Chopper, 10 Cups, Stainless Steel
products.verdict: Four functions and an easy-clean scraper in 10 cups.
products.description:
The 10-cup Hamilton Beach with a stainless steel blade is the middle of the line. It lists slicing, shredding, mincing and puree functions, plus an Easy Clean bowl scraper that helps you reach sticky purees without a spatula. Stainless steel holds an edge and resists staining from tomato or beet.

It ranks third because it holds two fewer cups than the 12-cup but adds the scraper and a clearer function list. Against the 8-cup version, it gives you extra room without paying more, and in the $50 to $100 tier it undercuts the Ninja by a wide margin.

Buy it for regular, moderate prep: weeknight slaw, sauces and chopped vegetables. The caveat is that the listing gives no motor wattage, so we cannot rate it for hard cheese or dough. Skip it if you want the strongest motor in the group.

products.name: KitchenAid 7-Cup Food Processor KFP0718
products.verdict: A full-size KitchenAid body for those moving up from a chopper.
products.description:
The KitchenAid KFP0718 is a full-size body with a 7-cup work bowl. It is the step up for owners who have outgrown a mini chopper and want a processor that carries a familiar name. The listing is short, giving only the bowl size and body type, and no price tier.

It ranks fourth because 7 cups is smaller than every Hamilton Beach model above it, and no wattage is listed. Much of the value here is brand, not specs. Compared with the 8-cup Hamilton Beach below, it gives you a cup less and a thinner spec list.

Buy it if you prefer the brand and 7 cups covers your cooking. Skip it if capacity or documented power drives your decision. Because the listing leaves out the price tier, check the current cost before ordering, and confirm which disks come in the box.
products.idealFor: Brand-loyal buyers moving up from a chopper.

products.name: Hamilton Beach 8 Cup Food Processor & Vegetable Chopper
products.description:
The 8-cup Hamilton Beach is the light-prep option. It lists slicing, shredding, mincing and pureeing functions plus a vegetable chopper mode, in the $50 to $100 tier. The smaller footprint suits shallow cabinets and small counters, and eight cups handles a family dinner.

It ranks fifth because the 10 and 12-cup models cost a similar amount and hold more, which makes the extra volume nearly free. What the 8-cup does offer is a narrower body that is easier to store and clean. It also gives you the same four functions as the 10-cup.

Choose it if you want to save space and money for other kitchen gear. Skip it if you batch cook, because large quantities will need several rounds. Like its siblings, it lists no wattage, so heavy tasks like shredding hard cheese are a question mark.
products.idealFor: Light home prep on a budget.

products.name: Cuisinart Small Food Processor, Auto-Reversing Smart Power Blade, 4-Cup
products.verdict: A 4-cup chopper with an auto-reversing blade.
products.description:
The Cuisinart is a compact chopper with an auto-reversing SmartPower blade. A 4-cup bowl, a small countertop footprint and a $25 to $50 price make it the cheapest and smallest unit here. The auto-reversing blade alternates direction, which helps it work through tangled herbs and onions without clumping.

It ranks last because it is a chopper at heart. No slicing or shredding function is listed, so it cannot replace the full-size machines for meal prep. In return it costs the least and takes the least space, which matters in a studio kitchen or a dorm.

Buy it for quick chopping jobs, salsa, garlic and herbs. Skip it if you need to slice cucumbers, shred carrots or process more than a small batch. Four cups limits you to small recipes, and that cap is the real caveat.

whatMatters.detail: Capacity is measured in cups. A 4 cup bowl suits chopping herbs and onions, while 9 to 12 cups handles meal prep and doubles of a recipe. A bigger bowl costs more storage and takes longer to clean. Check the listed cups and compare them to your usual batch, not your largest imagined one.

Wattage shows how well a motor handles dense foods like hard cheese, nuts and dough, and it decides whether a machine stalls under load. A weak motor also runs hot and wears out sooner. Peak watts can run higher than continuous watts, so read the label carefully. The Ninja BN601 lists 1000 peak watts. Find the figure in the spec bullets; a listing that hides it usually has little to show, so ask the seller.

Slicing, shredding, mincing and pureeing do different jobs, and each needs its own blade or disk. A chopper-only unit like the Cuisinart lacks them. The Hamilton Beach 10 and 8-cup list four functions. Check which blades and disks are in the box, and whether replacements are sold separately, because a missing shredding disk turns a processor into a chopper.

Tool-free systems like Stack & Snap are quicker to assemble than twist-lock designs, which can be fiddly with wet hands. Assembly matters because a machine that is annoying to build stays in the cabinet. Look at the listing photos and description for how the lid locks, and read for any safety interlock that stops the motor when the lid is not seated, which protects your fingers.

A bowl scraper and removable parts cut the effort of cleaning, because food processors collect residue in corners. Many bowls tolerate the dishwasher, but not all blades do. Check the care note in the listing, and look for features like the Easy Clean scraper on the 10-cup Hamilton Beach. Wide mouths and few crevices matter more than any wash-safe claim.

faq.q: Can I chop nuts in a food processor?
faq.a: Yes, but pulse in short bursts to avoid turning them into butter. A stronger motor like the Ninja BN601 helps, while the Cuisinart's 4 cups suits small amounts. Stop early, because chopped nuts keep breaking down.

faq.q: What is the biggest buying mistake?
faq.a: Choosing by wattage alone. Bowl size and included disks matter just as much, and several Hamilton Beach models list no wattage at all. Match capacity to your usual batch before comparing power, then check the disks.

faq.q: Is the Ninja worth it over Hamilton Beach?
faq.a: If you want presets and a stronger motor, yes. The Hamilton Beach 12-cup is cheaper for plain prep, and it holds three more cups than the Ninja's 9, so it wins on volume.

faq.q: How do I assemble a food processor?
faq.a: Seat the bowl, place the blade or disk, add the lid and lock it. Stack & Snap models like the Hamilton Beach 12-cup snap together without twisting, while others use twist locks. Read the manual once.

faq.q: How do I clean the parts?
faq.a: Hand wash blades carefully, since the edges are sharp, and check the listing for which parts are dishwasher safe. The 10-cup Hamilton Beach adds a bowl scraper to cut cleanup effort, which helps with sticky purees.

faq.q: Can a food processor replace a blender?
faq.a: Not fully. Processors chop and slice well, but blenders handle liquids better. The Ninja BN601 and Cuisinart can puree thick mixtures, yet a blender is still the tool for smoothies and soups.

finalTake: For most cooks, the Ninja BN601 is the best food processor under $200, with a 1000-peak-watt motor and presets. If capacity matters more, the Hamilton Beach 12-cup is the better value. Choose the 10-cup stainless model for regular prep, the KitchenAid for the brand, and the Cuisinart for quick chopping in a small kitchen.
